strengths: Unifying nine heterogeneous facial analysis tasks, including dense parsing, geometric estimation, and semantic prediction, addresses a useful deployment problem. The breadth of integration has value independently of achieving the best individual benchmark scores.

The reported results are competitive across several benchmarks: 3.52 MAE on BIWI, 3.05 NME on the 300W full set, and 91.83% attribute accuracy on CelebA. The 300VW category-C result, 6.75 versus STARLoss's 8.42, provides encouraging evidence of cross-dataset generalization.

The architecture is understandable at a high level, and backbone comparisons and supplementary ablations provide some design evidence. Dataset and loss attribution, augmentation details, and acknowledgment of retraining requirements and age/race prediction failures are useful.
weaknesses: Potential cross-task training/test overlap requires clarification. Head-pose training uses 300W-LP, which is derived from 300W imagery, while landmark evaluation uses 300W. The manuscript does not document exclusion of derivatives of landmark test images. This leaves an important uncertainty about the landmark comparisons; it is not evidence that leakage definitely occurred.

The central claim of resolving incompatible preprocessing is insufficiently demonstrated. Section 3.4 identifies landmark alignment versus head-pose preservation as a challenge, but Appendix E.2 still applies five-point alignment while E.3 uses loose crops. The paper should establish the accuracy of all tasks under one common inference preprocessing procedure. Unspecified loss weights and three additional training epochs for unspecified tasks also impede reproduction of the claimed joint model.

Table 2 contains a consequential numerical inconsistency: FaceXFormer's ten class F1 scores average to 91.01, not the reported 92.01. Under the displayed averaging convention, its advantage over Faceptor is 0.12 rather than 1.12 points. Performance remains competitive, but the headline margin needs correction or an explanation of the aggregation.

Architectural novelty is insufficiently distinguished from prior work. Task tokens already appear in cited facial generalists, and FaceX's token self-attention and bidirectional image–token cross-attention closely resemble SAM's two-way decoder. SAM is cited generally, but the decoder-level relationship and specific technical differences are not explained.

The ablations do not isolate the proposed mechanism's benefit. Table C.1 removes the entire decoder without explaining its replacement and produces severe performance collapse. Comparisons against a functional shared-backbone/task-head baseline and a standard decoder, under matched training, are needed to distinguish the proposed interactions from additional data and model capacity.

The efficiency evidence does not substantiate the parameter-efficient decoder claim. Table 5 compares backbones, but provides no matched decoder or prior multi-task runtime comparison. The 33.21 FPS measurement lacks inference hardware, batch size, and preprocessing scope, limiting interpretation of real-time deployment claims.

Evaluation coverage and demographic conclusions are overstated. No quantitative race-classification accuracy is reported, and the LFWA experiment evaluates only gender. Table 6 supports a small aggregate gender disparity, but FaceXFormer's age disparity of 0.50 exceeds CLIP's 0.30 and FaRL's 0.35, contradicting the blanket smallest-discrepancy claim. Aggregating six racial categories also cannot establish minimal bias across individual groups.
